title: Accounting Ratios
summary: A ratio expresses the relationship between two accounting figures. This chapter covers liquidity, solvency, activity (turnover) and profitability ratios: their formulas, what goes into each component, how to interpret them and how a transaction changes them.

notes.heading: Meaning, objectives and limitations
notes.html:
An accounting ratio is an arithmetical relationship between two related figures from the financial statements, expressed as a pure ratio (2:1), a percentage (25%), or times (5 times).

  • Objectives: simplify accounting data, assess liquidity, solvency, efficiency and profitability, enable intra-firm and inter-firm comparison, and help in forecasting.
  • Limitations: based on historical figures, ignore price-level changes and qualitative factors, affected by window dressing and differing accounting policies; a single ratio alone means little.

notes.heading: Liquidity ratios (short-term solvency)
notes.html:
RatioFormulaIdeal
Current RatioCurrent Assets ÷ Current Liabilities2 : 1
Quick (Liquid / Acid-test) RatioQuick Assets ÷ Current Liabilities1 : 1
  • Current assets: current investments, inventories (excluding loose tools and stores and spares), trade receivables (net of provision), cash and cash equivalents, short-term loans and advances, other current assets.
  • Current liabilities: short-term borrowings, trade payables, other current liabilities, short-term provisions.
  • Quick assets = Current assets − Inventories − Prepaid expenses.

Illustration 1

Current assets ₹6,00,000 (including inventories ₹1,50,000 and prepaid expenses ₹50,000); current liabilities ₹3,00,000.

Current ratio = 6,00,000 ÷ 3,00,000 = 2 : 1. Quick assets = 6,00,000 − 1,50,000 − 50,000 = 4,00,000; Quick ratio = 4,00,000 ÷ 3,00,000 = 1.33 : 1.

notes.heading: Solvency ratios (long-term)
notes.html:
RatioFormulaMeaning
Debt to EquityDebt ÷ Equity (Shareholders' Funds)Lower is safer; 2 : 1 is generally acceptable
Total Assets to DebtTotal Assets ÷ DebtHigher means more safety for lenders
Proprietary RatioShareholders' Funds ÷ Total AssetsHigher means less dependence on outsiders
Interest CoverageProfit before Interest and Tax ÷ Interest on long-term debtHigher means interest is well covered (in times)
  • Debt = Long-term borrowings + Long-term provisions.
  • Equity / Shareholders' funds = Share capital + Reserves and surplus = Non-current assets + Working capital − Non-current liabilities.

Illustration 2

Long-term borrowings ₹4,00,000; long-term provisions ₹1,00,000; share capital ₹8,00,000; reserves ₹2,00,000. Debt = 5,00,000; Equity = 10,00,000. Debt to equity = 0.5 : 1.

notes.heading: Activity (turnover) ratios
notes.html:
RatioFormula
Inventory TurnoverCost of Revenue from Operations ÷ Average Inventory
Trade Receivables TurnoverCredit Revenue from Operations ÷ Average Trade Receivables
Trade Payables TurnoverNet Credit Purchases ÷ Average Trade Payables
Working Capital TurnoverRevenue from Operations ÷ Working Capital
Fixed Assets TurnoverRevenue from Operations ÷ Net Fixed Assets
Net Assets (Capital Employed) TurnoverRevenue from Operations ÷ Capital Employed
  • Cost of revenue from operations = Revenue from operations − Gross profit = Opening inventory + Purchases + Direct expenses − Closing inventory.
  • Average inventory = (Opening + Closing) ÷ 2.
  • Trade receivables are taken before deducting provision for doubtful debts.
  • Average collection period = 12 months (or 365 days) ÷ Trade receivables turnover.

Illustration 3

Revenue ₹8,00,000; gross profit 25% on revenue; opening inventory ₹1,00,000; closing inventory ₹1,40,000.

Cost of revenue = 8,00,000 − 2,00,000 = 6,00,000. Average inventory = 1,20,000. Inventory turnover = 5 times.

notes.heading: Profitability ratios
notes.html:
RatioFormula
Gross Profit RatioGross Profit ÷ Revenue from Operations × 100
Operating Ratio(Cost of Revenue from Operations + Operating Expenses) ÷ Revenue from Operations × 100
Operating Profit RatioOperating Profit ÷ Revenue from Operations × 100 = 100 − Operating Ratio
Net Profit RatioNet Profit after Tax ÷ Revenue from Operations × 100
Return on Investment (ROI)Profit before Interest and Tax ÷ Capital Employed × 100
  • Operating expenses: employee benefits, depreciation, office, selling and distribution expenses. Non-operating items (interest on loans, loss on sale of assets, interest and dividend received) are excluded.
  • Capital employed = Shareholders' funds + Non-current liabilities = Non-current assets + Working capital.

Illustration 4

Profit before tax ₹3,00,000; interest on debentures ₹60,000; capital employed ₹18,00,000. PBIT = 3,60,000. ROI = 3,60,000 ÷ 18,00,000 × 100 = 20%.

notes.heading: Effect of transactions on ratios
notes.html:
Check what happens to the numerator and the denominator.

Current ratio isBoth CA and CL increase by the same amountBoth decrease by the same amount
More than 1 (e.g. 2 : 1)Ratio decreasesRatio improves
Equal to 1No changeNo change
Less than 1Ratio improvesRatio decreases
  • Payment to creditors (CA ↓, CL ↓) with ratio 2 : 1 → improves.
  • Purchase of goods on credit (CA ↑, CL ↑) with ratio 2 : 1 → declines.
  • Cash collected from debtors: one current asset replaces another → no change.
  • Purchase of machinery for cash: CA ↓, CL unchanged → declines.
  • Issue of shares for cash: CA ↑ → current ratio improves; debt-equity ratio falls.

Common mistakes: including inventories in quick assets; using revenue instead of cost of revenue for inventory turnover; treating interest on loans as an operating expense; using profit after tax for ROI.

keyTerms.definition: Ability of a business to meet its short-term obligations as they fall due.
Ability of a business to meet its long-term obligations.
Current assets less inventories and prepaid expenses.
Shareholders' funds plus non-current liabilities; also non-current assets plus working capital.
Revenue from operations less gross profit; the direct cost of goods sold.
Revenue from operations less cost of revenue from operations and operating expenses.
A ratio showing how many times an asset or liability is turned over in relation to revenue or cost.

formulas.name: Quick ratio
formulas.html: (Current Assets − Inventories − Prepaid Expenses) ÷ Current Liabilities

formulas.name: Interest coverage ratio
formulas.html: Profit before Interest and Tax ÷ Interest on Long-term Debt

formulas.name: Inventory turnover ratio
formulas.html: Cost of Revenue from Operations ÷ Average Inventory

formulas.name: Trade receivables turnover ratio
formulas.html: Credit Revenue from Operations ÷ Average Trade Receivables

formulas.name: Trade payables turnover ratio
formulas.html: Net Credit Purchases ÷ Average Trade Payables

formulas.name: Operating ratio
formulas.html: (Cost of Revenue from Operations + Operating Expenses) ÷ Revenue from Operations × 100

formulas.name: Net profit ratio
formulas.html: Net Profit after Tax ÷ Revenue from Operations × 100

formulas.name: Return on investment
formulas.html: Profit before Interest and Tax ÷ Capital Employed × 100

mcqs.q:
Assertion (A): A very high current ratio is not always desirable.
Reason (R): It may indicate idle funds, slow-moving inventories or poor collection from debtors.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcqs.explanation: Excess current assets earn little, so a very high ratio signals inefficient use of funds.

questions.q: What does a low inventory turnover ratio indicate?
questions.answerHtml: It indicates that inventory is moving slowly: over-stocking, obsolete goods or weak sales, with funds blocked in inventory.

questions.q: Current liabilities of a company are ₹3,00,000. Its current ratio is 3 : 1 and quick ratio is 1 : 1. Calculate the value of inventories (there are no prepaid expenses).
questions.answerHtml:
Current assets = 3 × 3,00,000 = ₹9,00,000.

Quick assets = 1 × 3,00,000 = ₹3,00,000.

Inventories = Current assets − Quick assets = ₹6,00,000.

questions.q: Revenue from operations ₹12,00,000 (cash revenue being 25% of total); opening trade receivables ₹1,20,000; closing trade receivables ₹1,80,000. Calculate the trade receivables turnover ratio and the average collection period.
questions.answerHtml:
Credit revenue = 75% of 12,00,000 = ₹9,00,000.

Average trade receivables = (1,20,000 + 1,80,000) ÷ 2 = ₹1,50,000.

Turnover ratio = 9,00,000 ÷ 1,50,000 = 6 times.

Average collection period = 12 ÷ 6 = 2 months.

questions.q: The debt to equity ratio of a company is 1 : 2. State with reasons whether it will increase, decrease or not change when: (i) equity shares of ₹2,00,000 are issued for cash; (ii) machinery of ₹1,00,000 is bought on long-term deferred payment; (iii) a bank loan of ₹50,000 (long-term) is repaid; (iv) goods of ₹40,000 are bought on credit.
questions.answerHtml:
• (i) Decrease: equity rises, debt unchanged.
  • (ii) Increase: long-term debt rises, equity unchanged.
  • (iii) Decrease: debt falls, equity unchanged.
  • (iv) No change: a current asset and a current liability rise; neither debt nor equity is affected.
